title: Knee aspiration: suspected septic arthritis
stem: Cubicle 20. Mr Patel, 39, has a hot, swollen, painful right knee with fever and rigors for 2 days. He has post-traumatic arthritis of that knee; no joint replacement. Temperature 38.9 °C. Aspirate the knee on the model and explain what you will send the fluid for.
notes:
Checked against the BSR/BOA guideline on the management of the hot swollen joint in adults (2006, reaffirmed), NICE CKS (septic arthritis), and standard aspiration technique.

A hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proved otherwise: aspirate before antibiotics (unless it delays them in sepsis), send for Gram stain, culture, white cell count and crystals; take blood cultures. Empirical antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin, or per local guidance; cover gonococcus in sexually active young adults) once samples are taken; orthopaedic referral for washout. Prosthetic joints are aspirated by orthopaedics in theatre conditions. Overlying cellulitis is a contraindication at that site; anticoagulation is not an absolute contraindication.

Technique: consent, asepsis, knee extended and relaxed; lateral (or medial) approach 1 cm superior and lateral to the superolateral patella edge (or at mid-patella under its lateral border), angled under the patella; local anaesthetic to skin; aspirate with a 19–21 G needle; do not inject steroid. Your notes describe a site 2 cm lateral to the patella and 'milk the fluid', which is compatible. Crystals are not proof against sepsis: both can coexist.
